query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy, incorporating a minor amount (~5 at.%) of aluminum will promote the in-situ formation of a finely dispersed, coherent γ′ (Ni3Ti-type) precipitate within the FCC matrix, thereby enhancing the alloy’s elevated-temperature yield strength and resistance to coarsening compared to the same alloy without aluminum addition.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy where titanium and nickel are the primary constituents (with the remaining elements present in 5–35 at% each and comparable atomic radii) forming a predominantly FCC solid solution.
generation.intervention: Addition of approximately 5 at.% aluminum to the baseline titanium–nickel primary alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Testing under elevated-temperature conditions (around 800 °C) in order to assess yield strength, thermal stability, and phase coarsening behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a two-phase microstructure consisting of a disordered FCC matrix with a fine, coherent γ′ (ordered Ni3Ti-type) precipitate phase.
generation.mechanism: The aluminum addition is expected to trigger a precipitation hardening mechanism by stabilizing a γ′ phase that is coherent with the FCC matrix. This phase acts as a barrier to dislocation motion at high temperatures, reducing creep and maintaining yield strength via solid solution and interphase boundary strengthening.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aluminum-modified alloy should exhibit a higher specific yield strength and better coarsening resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the unmodified, single-phase solid solution alloy.
generation.baseline: The original titanium–nickel primary HEA without the aluminum addition, which lacks the beneficial γ′ precipitate-induced strengthening mechanism.
generation.boundary: The intervention applies to high-entropy alloys that satisfy the compositional criteria (each element at 5–35 at%) and are processed to attain a predominantly FCC structure; the effect is targeted for operating temperatures around 800 °C where the γ/γ′ microstructure is stable.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal aluminum concentration and processing route (e.g., cooling rate and heat-treatment duration) necessary to maximize the volume fraction and stability of the γ′ phase require further experimental calibration. Additionally, interactions with any other minor alloying elements may modulate the precipitate formation and overall high-temperature performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys with titanium and nickel as primary constituents that meet high-entropy criteria. One set will be produced with an additional 5 at.% aluminum, while the control set will have no aluminum addition. Both alloy sets shall be fabricated under identical conditions (e.g., via directed energy deposition or casting) and subjected to identical post-processing heat treatments aimed at obtaining comparable grain sizes and phase distributions. Mechanical testing (e.g., compression or tensile tests) should then be performed at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (~800 °C). Microstructural characterization (using SEM, TEM, and XRD) should be conducted to verify the formation, volume fraction, and coherence of the γ′ precipitates.
measurements: Yield strength and specific yield strength at elevated temperature (around 800 °C)
Phase identification and precipitate size/distribution via TEM/XRD
Grain size and microstructural coarsening rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-added alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant higher yield strength and improved phase stability (i.e., retention of a fine, coherent γ′ phase) at elevated temperatures compared to the baseline alloy, or if the expected γ′ phase is not observed in microstructural analysis, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The addition of elements with similar metallic atomic radii but different crystallographic structures (Al and Ti) to the Co-Ni-Fe alloy caused higher solution strengthening by the element with a different crystallographic structure than the solvent. The solid solution strengthening coming from addition of 5 at. pct Al to the Co-Ni-Fe alloy is negligible, while the addition of 5 at. pct of Ti significantly increases the solid solution strengthening. The precipitation hardening effect related to the presence of (CoNi)3Ti phase caused by the addition of 5 at. pct Ti is comparable with the total effect of the 5 at. pct Al and 5 at. pct Ti addition, which caused the precipitation of γ′ ((NiCo)3AlTi). Precipitation hardening is much greater in the investigated alloys than the solid solution hardening. We showed a successful way for effectively strengthening the FCC-HEA system (NiCoFe) using a small Ti addition. The microstructure obtained in the M3 alloy consists of precipitates with an L12 structure and structurally coherent with FCC matrix. We showed one of the ways of searching for new high-entropy alloys.

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) have drawn significant attention due to their unique design and superior mechanical properties. Comprising 5–35 at% of five or more elements with similar atomic radii, HEAs exhibit high configurational entropy, resulting in single-phase solid solutions rather than intermetallic compounds. Additive manufacturing (AM), particularly direct energy deposition (DED), is effective for producing HEAs due to its rapid cooling rates, which ensure uniform microstructures and minimize defects. These alloys typically form face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structures, contributing to their exceptional strength, hardness, and mechanical performance across various temperatures. However, FCC-structured HEAs often have low yield strengths, posing a challenge for structural applications. In this study, a Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA was manufactured using the DED method. This study proposes that the addition of aluminum and titanium creates a γ + γ′ phase structure within a multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix, enhancing the thermal stability and coarsening the resistance and strength. The matrix phase of the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA appeared as the γ phase of the FCC structure, and the γ′ phase of the ordered FCC structure was confirmed to be widely distributed in the form of dot-like pores. In addition, no additional precipitated phases appeared on the SEM images, and it was confirmed that the grain size of the γ phase was coarse. Figure 7c,d show the results of the EDS analysis of the deposited Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA for the γ and γ′ phases, respectively. The analysis confirmed that the Ni-rich γ phase solid solution with Al and Ti was formed first, followed by the formation of the γ′ phase solid solution with a (Ni, Co)3(Ti, Al) composition.
